title: Congruences & the Euclidean algorithm
subject: Pure Mathematics
summary: Everything here grows from one idea, division with a remainder. It defines congruence, it drives Euclid’s algorithm for the greatest common divisor, and it lets you solve equations in whole numbers.

notes.title: Division with a remainder
notes.text: A whole number splits into copies of a divisor plus a leftover: a = bq + r with 0 ≤ r < b. The quotient q counts the copies and the remainder r is what is left. Example: {a} ÷ {b} gives {q} copies with {r} left over.
points: The remainder is always smaller than the divisor.
notes.hint: Find how many whole copies of the divisor fit, multiply back, then see what is left.

fb.{s}: That is the quotient. The remainder is what is left after {d} × {s}.

working: The remainder is {t}, and it is smaller than {d}.

notes.title: Congruence (mod n)
notes.text: Two numbers are congruent modulo n when they leave the same remainder on division by n. Write a ≡ b (mod n). Another way to say it: n divides a − b. Example: {a1} and {a2} both leave remainder {r} on division by {n}, so {a1} ≡ {a2} (mod {n}).
notes.hint: Work out the remainder of the given number first, then look for the option with the same remainder.

notes.title: Euclid’s algorithm
notes.text: The greatest common divisor gcd(a, b) is the largest whole number that divides both. Divide, then replace (a, b) by (b, r) and repeat until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero remainder is the gcd. Example first step: {E} = {e1} × {F} + {e2}, so gcd({E}, {F}) = gcd({F}, {e2}).
points: Each step shrinks the numbers, so it always finishes.
notes.hint: Do one division: how many times does the smaller number fit into the larger, and what is left?

notes.title: Linear congruences
notes.text: To solve ax ≡ c (mod n) when gcd(a, n) = 1, first find the inverse a⁻¹: the number with a × a⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod n). Bézout guarantees it exists, because whole numbers x₀, y satisfy a·x₀ + n·y = 1. Then x ≡ a⁻¹ × c. Example: {a} × {i0} − {n} × {y0} = 1, so the inverse of {a} (mod {n}) is {i0}.
